Data: The raw data that you want to plot.

4.2 Examples
Let’s go through some examples to illustrate how ggplot can be used to create different types of visualizations.

4.2.1 Scatter Plot
Creating a scatter plot to explore the relationship between two variables, say mpg (miles per gallon) and wt (weight of the car) from the mtcars dataset.


Code
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + 
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Weight of Car", y = "Miles Per Gallon",
       title = "Scatter plot of MPG vs Car Weight")









This code block creates a scatter plot where car weight is on the x-axis and miles per gallon on the y-axis. Each point represents a car.


4.2.2 Bar Chart
Creating a bar chart to show the count of cars by the number of cylinders.


Code
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(cyl))) + 
  geom_bar() + 
  labs(x = "Number of Cylinders", y = "Count",
       title = "Count of Cars by Cylinders")









This plots a bar chart where each bar represents the count of cars with a certain number of cylinders.


4.2.3 Line Graph
Plotting a line graph, assuming we have a time series data.frame economics that is part of ggplot2 package.


Code
ggplot(economics, aes(x = date, y = unemploy)) + 
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Number of Unemployed Persons",
       title = "Unemployment over Time") 









This code plots the unemployment numbers over time, with time on the x-axis and the number of unemployed persons on the y-axis.


4.2.4 Faceted Plot
Creating a faceted plot to compare scatter plots of mpg vs wt across different numbers of cylinders.


Code
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + 
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~cyl) +
  labs(title = "MPG vs Weight by Number of Cylinders")









This splits the data into subsets based on the number of cylinders and creates a scatter plot for each subset.

section: 5.2 Fit a simple linear regression model (reg_short)
text:
5.2 Fit a simple linear regression model (reg_short)

lm(hwy ~ displ, data = mpg) estimates the relationship between:

Outcome (y): hwy = highway miles per gallon
Predictor (x): displ = engine displacement (engine size)

In equation form:

\(hwy_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 displ_i + u_i\)

Interpretation:

\(\beta_1\) tells how much expected highway MPG changes when displ increases by 1 unit
(holding nothing else constant, because nothing else is included).

title: Linear Regression
section: 5.3 Fit a multiple linear regression model (reg_long)
text:
5.3 Fit a multiple linear regression model (reg_long)

lm(hwy ~ displ + class, data = mpg) adds class (vehicle class) as an additional predictor.
In equation form:

\(hwy_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 displ_i + \text{(class effects)} + u_i\)

Important detail: class is a categorical variable.

R automatically converts it into dummy variables (indicators).
One class becomes the reference (baseline) category.
Each reported class coefficient measures the difference in expected hwy
compared with that baseline class, holding displ fixed.




5.3.1 4) Print the regression table

stargazer(reg_short, reg_long, type = "html") prints both models side-by-side.
Because type = "html", stargazer outputs HTML (best for Quarto/HTML documents).
The chunk option #| results: asis tells Quarto to render the HTML as a table
rather than showing the raw HTML text.

reg_short answers: How is highway MPG associated with engine displacement (overall)?
reg_long answers: How is highway MPG associated with displacement after comparing within vehicle classes?
Adding class can change the displ coefficient because vehicle type is related to both
engine size and MPG.

Many organizations store data in databases (MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, etc.)

filter rows (WHERE)
select columns (SELECT)
aggregate (GROUP BY)
join tables (JOIN)

R (or Python) is then used for modeling, visualization, and reporting.

text:
Questions 3–8 (Regression models)
You will estimate three linear regression models for:

Outcome: \(\log(\text{price\_floz})\)

Reference levels (required):

Set "BUD_LIGHT" as the reference level for brand.
Set "BUFFALO-ROCHESTER" as the reference level for market.

There are \(N+1\) distinct categories in market.




Model 1
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log(\text{price\_floz}) = &\ \beta_{0} + \sum_{i=1}^{N} \beta_{i} \,\text{market}_{i} + \sum_{j=N+1}^{N+4} \beta_{j} \,\text{brand}_{j}
+ \beta_{N+5} \,\text{container\_CAN} \\
&\,+\, \beta_{N+6} \log(\text{beer\_floz}) + \epsilon
\end{aligned}
\]


Model 2 (brand-specific volume sensitivity)
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log(\text{price\_floz}) \,=\, & \beta_{0} \,+\, \sum_{i=1}^{N}\beta_{i}\,\text{market}_{i} \,+\, \sum_{j=N+1}^{N+4}\beta_{j}\,\text{brand}_{j} \,+\, \beta_{N+5}\,\text{container\_CAN} \\
&\,+\, \beta_{N+6}\log(\text{beer\_floz})\\
&\,+\, \sum_{j=N+1}^{N+4}\beta_{j\times\text{beer\_floz}}\,\text{brand}_{j}\times \log(\text{beer\_floz})\\
&\,+\, \epsilon
\end{aligned}
\]


Model 3 (promo + brand-specific promo effects)
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log(\text{price\_floz}) \,=\, & \beta_{0} \,+\, \sum_{i=1}^{N}\beta_{i}\,\text{market}_{i} \,+\, \sum_{j=N+1}^{N+4}\beta_{j}\,\text{brand}_{j} \,+\, \beta_{N+5}\,\text{container\_CAN} \\
&\,+\, \beta_{N+6}\log(\text{beer\_floz})\\
&\,+\, \beta_{N+7}\,\text{promo} \times\log(\text{beer\_floz}) \\
&\,+\, \sum_{j=N+1}^{N+4}\beta_{j\times\text{beer\_floz}}\,\text{brand}_{j}\times \log(\text{beer\_floz})\\
&\,+\, \sum_{j=N+1}^{N+4}\beta_{j\times\text{promo}}\,\text{brand}_{j}\times \text{promo}\\
&\,+\, \sum_{j=N+1}^{N+4}\beta_{j\times\text{promo}\times\text{beer\_floz}}\,\text{brand}_{j}\times \text{promo}\times \log(\text{beer\_floz})\\
&\,+\, \epsilon
\end{aligned}
\]


Question 3 — Model intuition (conceptual)
For each model, explain in plain English:

What is the model trying to capture?
What kinds of differences across markets and brands are allowed?
How does the model treat the relationship between volume (beer_floz) and price (price_floz)?
What new flexibility is added when moving from Model 1 → 2 → 3?

Answer: # Model 1 is trying to capture price per fluid ounce # Model 2 is capturing price per fluid ounce in regards to brand specific volume sensitivity # Model 3 is capturing price per fluid ounce in regards to volume sensitivity and promo effects # Nrand differences in price levels and pricing behaviors are allowed in the model # There is a log-log relationship, meaning the coefficient on log(beer_floz) is associated with elasticity. # New flexibility being added is volume sensitivity in Model 2 and promotion effect in Model 3


Question 4 — Estimate, predict, and evaluate
Using beer_train:

Fit Model 1, Model 2, and Model 3 using lm().
Provide a regression table or summary() output for each model.
Using beer_test, generate out-of-sample predictions:

predict \(\log(\text{price\_floz})\)
convert predictions back to price_floz using exp()

Evaluate predictive performance on beer_test:

report RMSE (required)


Requirements:

Present results in a small table comparing Model 1–3 test RMSE.
Briefly comment on which model predicts best and by how much.

Answer:

beer_train <- beer_train %>%
  mutate(
    brand = relevel(factor(brand), ref = "BUD_LIGHT"),
    market = relevel(factor(market), ref = "BUFFALO-ROCHESTER"),
    container = factor(container),
    promo = factor(promo)
  )

beer_test <- beer_test %>%
  mutate(
    brand = relevel(factor(brand), ref = "BUD_LIGHT"),
    market = relevel(factor(market), ref = "BUFFALO-ROCHESTER"),
    container = factor(container),
    promo = factor(promo)
  )
beer_train <- beer_train %>%
  mutate(
    log_price = log(price_floz),
    log_volume = log(beer_floz)
  )

beer_test <- beer_test %>%
  mutate(
    log_price = log(price_floz),
    log_volume = log(beer_floz)
  )


model1 <- lm(
  log_price ~ market + brand + container + log_volume,
  data = beer_train
)
summary(model1)


model2 <- lm(
  log_price ~ market + brand + container +
    log_volume + brand:log_volume,
  data = beer_train
)
summary(model2)


model3 <- lm(
  log_price ~ market + container +
    brand * promo * log_volume,
  data = beer_train
)
summary(model3)


# predict()
pred1_log <- predict(model1, newdata = beer_test)
pred1 <- exp(pred1_log)
pred2_log <- predict(model2, newdata = beer_test)
pred2 <- exp(pred2_log)
pred3_log <- predict(model3, newdata = beer_test)
pred3 <- exp(pred3_log)


# rmse
rmse <- function(actual, predicted) {
  sqrt(mean((actual - predicted)^2))
}
rmse1 <- rmse(beer_test$price_floz, pred1)
rmse2 <- rmse(beer_test$price_floz, pred2)
rmse3 <- rmse(beer_test$price_floz, pred3)

rmse1
rmse2
rmse3

Across the three models, analyze how sensitive price is to volume, and how that differs by brand and promo:

In Model 1, explain what the coefficient on \(\log(\text{beer\_floz})\) means.
In Model 2, show how the volume sensitivity differs by brand.
